utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One small matter before we begin. Apparently Exhibit Z1198.5 was in the bundle of exhibits that were returned to the Prosecution, Mr. President, but the registrar has a note that it's been entered into evidence, and it should be returned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's already admitted. I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You returned the exhibits to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- but somehow this document tiptoed into evidence, according to the registrar's record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- but it should be returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask the usher to put this document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is one reference to you in the UNPROFOR documents that have been introduced into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, this is Exhibit D334/1, tab 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's in English, Colonel, and on page 5 your name is mentioned, although wrongly spelled. "Marinko Palabera," it says there, "Chief of Military Police. He is assessed to be professional and serious about his job." But just above that, sir, is a reference to the HVO brigade commander in Busovaca, a man by the name of Dusko Grubesic. And there's no question, Colonel, that throughout your time as chief of military police, from August until he was replaced in October, he was actually the military commander of the HVO in Busovaca. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can remember, Dusko Grubesic was the commander of the HVO brigade in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was replaced as military commander in Busovaca in October of 1993 by a man called Jure Cavara. Is that consistent with your recollection, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Commander Grubesic, I believe, is now a brigadier in the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dusko Grubesic at the moment is the commander -- Just a moment. He is the commander of the Vitez unit, or the Vitez formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One question that I omitted to ask you yesterday, Colonel, is this: You have had the opportunity to review your testimony in the Blaskic case on January 11th and 12th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't stay there long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a formal question for you, Colonel. Do you reaffirm the factual accuracy of the testimony that you gave before the Blaskic trial court a year and a half -- well, a year and ten months ago?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. We covered yesterday Mr. Kordic and his absence from the chain of command, and I'd like to continue questions along the lines of inquiring into the chain of command while you were commander of the military police. There's no question that the military commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and the principal military figure in that zone was your superior, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And up until the date that the Washington Agreement was signed, Colonel, and indeed even before you became military police commander, you received your orders directly from the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in no sense, sir, were you a subordinate of or answerable to Mr. Kordic at any time during the tenure -- during your tenure of office as military police commander?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One matter of detail which could become relevant in my later questions: You took over your duties as military police commander while the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna was still in existence, the HZ HB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was founded about a month after you were appointed as a military police commander, the republic being declared on August the 28th, 1993. Is that consistent with your recollection, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during the course of your -- the performance of your duties as commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, Colonel Blaskic required you to attend daily briefings with him each morning. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And on each Friday, weekly meetings were held with all of the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's also fair to say, sir, that at no time were any of the individuals whose names were mentioned to you by Mr. Scott yesterday, a couple of examples being Miso Mijic and Dragan Voloder, at no time were they permitted to attend meetings of the military bodies in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, were they?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, if we take a look at exhibit number eight of the exhibit package that we identified yesterday as Exhibit D344/1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no need to put it on the ELMO, but I would be obliged if you would give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is a letter or a reply by Colonel Blaskic, dated September the 11th, 1993. We don't know who it's a reply to, but it responds to a request -- actually, it's to the Central Bosnia so-called Security and Information Service centre, the SIS centre, about which we heard yesterday. And Colonel Blaskic responds to a request made to attend Central Bosnia Operative Zone command meetings, and he refuses that request. Were you familiar with that refusal, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I see this reply of Colonel Blaskic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Since you are unfamiliar with the document, there's no need to go through it other than this: On page 2, Colonel Blaskic tells the SIS centre that, "I do not know, nor have I been informed, either what is within the competence of the SIS centre or what authority its individual staff members have, including the post of the chief of the centre, since I have not received any orders or instructions." That's the statement of your commander, sir, and the same is true of you. You were completely unaware that the so-called SIS centre, whatever it was, had any official function whatsoever in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite, Your Honours. Yesterday I said that Colonel Blaskic in the Operative Zone Central Bosnia had his own assistant for security affairs, and I communicated with him, or rather, we cooperated. And the SIS centre was something that I did not know at all about at that time. It was only through the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll have some questions for you later about these individuals, Mijic and Voloder, but let me continue on with the briefings that you attended every morning with Blaskic. During those briefings, you would get your daily orders from your commanding officer, wouldn't you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes. Following briefings, Colonel Blaskic would give tasks, not only to me as the commander of the military police, but to all his assistants, depending on our mandates and whatever we were in charge of; that is, we would all be issued with tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've previously explained to us how difficult the situation was with many of your subordinate military policemen on the front lines. Occasionally, the orders that you would receive from your commanding officer would be combat orders, too, wouldn't they, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were the military police which went to the defence line. We were at the defence lines most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But the particular combat directives that you received for the operation of your soldiers on the defence lines, Colonel, were given to you by Colonel Blaskic during either these daily briefings that you attended with him or the weekly commanders meetings that he convened every Friday?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- we did not have -- while I was the commander of the police, we did not have any combat orders. All we had was the defence, that is, holding defence lines in the areas of operation of Muslim forces. Where there is a certain front, or rather, where it is broken through, we would go to replenish it, to fill it in, and we would take those trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, Colonel, and maybe my question was inelegantly phrased, but can we both agree that any orders that you received for military activity of a defensive nature were received from your commanding officer, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kordic never attended any of these daily briefings or these weekly commanders meetings that were convened by Colonel Blaskic. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that is how morning briefings were, not Colonel -- that is, at Colonel Blaskic's, Mr. Kordic was not present; but at briefings which were held every Friday or -- yes, I mean every Friday, once or twice he did attend. I did see Mr. Kordic. He was there in those meetings, but he was only present there. That is, he did not conduct those briefings, he was simply present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So during the eight months that you were a military police commander, between the date that you assumed your duties on August the 1st of 1993 until the end of March of 1994 when the Washington Agreement was signed, your recollection is that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your recollection is that Mr. Kordic attended only one or two of those meetings that were held every week?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. And I should also like to tell the Court I remember well when Mr. Kordic was present, that I, having received the duty of the commander of the 4th Battalion, at that time, at that meeting, I said that we had knowledge, that we had, that is, knowledge that our criminals will sell both Blaskic and Kordic to the Muslim side for 50 to 100.000 marks. I said that at the meeting and I remember that Mr. Kordic was present at that very meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But Mr. Kordic never made any military observations at any of these meetings, or comments of a military nature. That would be fair to say and you would agree with that, Colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these briefings were conducted by Colonel Blaskic, because those were military briefings. And Mr. Kordic was simply present, and naturally he took notes, he wrote, but he made no comments about any military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few final questions on this topic. You told us yesterday that you yourself never once received any orders from Mr. Kordic, or instructions or directives. It's true also that none of your subordinates ever told you that Mr. Kordic had tried to issue orders or directives to them either; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, you were shown some documents yesterday relating to police appointments and so forth. One of them was Exhibit Z386, signed by your then-commander, Ivo Rezo, on January 21st, 1993. It was an order that supposedly evidenced the appointment of Nikola Perica to the post of commander of the Fojnica police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, this was -- the post itself, commander of the Fojnica police Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. station, was actually a civilian post, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you have a recollection, Colonel, that in fact Mr. Perica was never -- he never took up the post of commander of the Fojnica police station, for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know Ivica -- Ivo -- no, sorry. No. This is Nikola Perica. I don't know the man, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked some questions yesterday about the group known as the Jokers and also the 3rd Light Assault Battalion. Would you agree that no one throughout your many years as commander of military police in Vitez has ever suggested to you that the Jokers were ever under the authority or command in any way of Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that, of course, includes your long-time deputy, Vladimir Santic, doesn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Santic never said ... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could give the witness the big book of military police exhibits that the Prosecution introduced yesterday. And since the book itself doesn't have a single exhibit reference, could I just recite the exhibit numbers for the record that are in this binder, Your Honour? It's Exhibit Z1134, 1134.1, 1165.2, 2332, and 2340. Actually, I've marked this up. Do we have the original exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter if you've marked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there's anything of particular importance to yourself on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's a little bit, but I'll try to remember what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I want to suggest to you, Colonel, that there is in all of these military police documents no reference to Mr. Kordic having any command role or any authority whatsoever in the military police or any of its component units, including the Jokers and the 3rd Light Assault Battalion. And I am also going to suggest to you, and I'd like your comment on this, that the reason for the omission of Mr. Kordic's name in those documents is because he had no such command authority, such command role, any kind of superior/subordinate relationship insofar as the military police are concerned. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would agree with this. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's just a few documents, or just two documents in this package that I'd like you to look at. Unfortunately, they are both in English, so the usher is going to have to put them on the ELMO for everybody's reference, and I'll translate for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first is tabbed at the top with a yellow tab, Mr. Usher. This is Exhibit Z2332A, Your Honours, at page 11. And we'll start with the dissolution of the 3rd Light Assault Battalion first and then go into the process by which it was created. But the document that I want to draw to your attention is -- it was marked at the top, Mr. Usher, with the yellow tab, page 11. Yes. And I've highlighted the portion at the bottom of the page. There you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This describes how the 1st and 2nd Light Assault Battalions ceased to exist as a result of an order issued by Lieutenant General Anto Roso, and we can see that the document makes the same reference insofar as the 3rd Light Assault Battalion is concerned. Is it your recollection that the 3rd Light Assault Battalion was in fact dissolved by order of General Roso, the then-commander of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know. I mean, I know nothing about it. I know that the 3rd Light Assault -- or rather, that parts of the 3rd Light Assault created the 3rd Guards Brigade. That is what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm through with that one. The next document is also marked at the top. This is Exhibit 2332I, I believe, Your Honour, and it's a report that's actually issued by Pasko Ljubicic, or authored by Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It says, sir, that Mr. Vukovic used to be the 4th Battalion of Military Police commander. He was then replaced by Pasko Ljubicic on the orders of Valentin Coric, who was the chief of the military police administration in Ljubuski. And that's correct; that's a correct recitation of fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Zvonko Vukovic, it was the commander, Pasko Ljubicic, and I succeeded him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then Mr. Ljubicic goes on to recite the locations in which the 4th Battalion of Military Police participated in military activity and identifies Ahmici as one of those areas. Did you ever discuss the operations conducted by the 4th Battalion of Military Police in Ahmici with your predecessor, Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that package of exhibits. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have a document for the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the package of exhibits that I had asked you to review, Exhibit D343/1 -- no, I'm sorry. It's D344/1. I apologise for that. Just so that we can finish out our inquiries relating to the 3rd Light Assault Battalion, sir, would you take a look at the very first tab of this exhibit. It's an order dated June 28th, 1993, and it's an order signed by -- or for Valentin Coric, the commander of the military police administration in Ljubuski. And in this order, he directs the 3rd Light Assault Military Police Battalion, based in Vitez, to be formed. Were you aware that Mr. Coric had issued that order in June of 1993 or did you become aware of this order at any time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you'd just turn -- or just turn to the bottom of the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for the Court's information, it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This order from Mr. Coric goes on to recite that the assistant chief of the military police administration responsible for the zone was also authorised to command the Light Assault Battalion in that zone. So Mr. Ljubicic would have been authorised to command the 3rd Light Assault Battalion in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. Is that consistent with your understanding, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And if you would just turn to tab 5 of this exhibit package.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this has already been marked, Your Honours, as Exhibit Z1165.2. There's an attachment to an order, another order by Mr. Coric, dated August the 12th, 1993, that recites Mr. Ljubicic having been appointed as assistant chief of the military police administration for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and that's a correct recitation. When you assumed your duties as military police commander of the 4th Battalion, Mr. Ljubicic was actually the assistant chief of the military police administration in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So at all times, as far as you're aware, at least prior to the dissolution of the 3rd Light Assault Battalion by order of General Roso, that unit, that combat unit was under the direct authority and command of Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And never under the authority or command in any way whatsoever of Mr. Kordic, as far as you're aware, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've given some testimony, Colonel, regarding the difficulties between the military police and the criminals that simply abounded in your area in the anarchic times of the autumn and winter of 1993. You suspected your own assistant commander Mr. Jozipovic, I think you said yesterday, of basically tipping off criminal elements to anticipated or planned criminal investigations or investigation activities by the military police, and that's why you removed him. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also mentioned an individual by the name of Zarko Andric who had the nickname of Zuti. Now, Zuti was shot by his deputy or his assistant, a man by the name of Zoran Tuka, shot and paralysed correct, in a murder attempt?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There has been some suggestion in some of the papers, Colonel -- maybe you can throw some light on this because I simply don't know -- is it the case that this fellow Zuti was wounded as the military police were trying to arrest him, or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Immediately after this murder attempt on Zuti, the man that you were asked about yesterday, Miso Mijic, fled to Mostar, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't remember exactly when Miso Mijic left, but not only he but his assistants, or rather, those who were with him, went to Herzegovina. I don't remember exactly when, but I know it was very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And would you agree that they left in one almighty hurry, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in connection with this rampant criminal activity that unfortunately pervaded your area of responsibility, sir, you yourself were the victim of crimes, weren't you? You had your car stolen a couple of times, I believe. You even had explosives placed under your car once to blow it up in an apparent murder attempt on you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my car was not stolen. The first time they took my car by an RPG, and that was one of Zuti's men; and the second time they put an explosive underneath my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Court might be wondering, Colonel, and I certainly am, that if this criminal activity was perpetrated upon you yourself, the commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, why wasn't it that this perpetrator Zuti was arrested and prosecuted for that? Was that a practical alternative or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time, that couldn't be done. Judge Picinovic [phoen], who was at the court in Vitez, he was wounded by Zuti, and he didn't want to submit a criminal report. And the public prosecutor's car was stolen, Marinko Jurcevic car, and again, that was done by Zuti's men, and again, there was no criminal report. Before I took up the duty of the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, Zuti attacked military police units twice, and there was no punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the question is, Colonel, why not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that at that time there were widespread attacks by the Muslim forces, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on Central Bosnia, and the chief priority was to defend the lines, the defence lines, and I think that was why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's turn to another subject, Colonel. You've told us that Colonel Blaskic could request the military police to perform investigations into suspected criminal transgressions, but he could not himself order arrests or influence the manner in which the investigation was actually conducted. Is that -- do I have it correctly? Do I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And on occasion, Colonel Blaskic did exercise that power. He did request you to perform criminal investigations into suspected criminal activity, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to what he knew at the morning briefings, he would say that such and such should be investigated. It all depended on what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kordic never had that power and never once requested you to perform any investigation, right? That was outside of his ambit, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you're familiar, I take it, sir, with the rules of military discipline that permitted military commanders and brigade commanders, depending upon their rank, to issue on their own authority disciplinary punishments against people who had transgressed the rules of military discipline, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I think you yourself had the authority equivalent to a brigade commander, and that enabled you to impose disciplinary detention sentences of up to one month upon transgressors?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And just three documents I would like to go over very lightly with you, Colonel, which show that you were actually performing your job and that charges were being filed, investigations were being performed. Tab 4 of the package in front of you is a report that you prepared, I believe, dated August the 10th, 1993. And the only point I want to draw to your attention is that, amongst other things, it says that criminal charges were filed against two Croats, Davor Lovric and Marinko Stojanovic, because they had been suspected of committing the crime of rape. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a lot of time has elapsed. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's just one point about the document, but the real point that I wanted to make, Colonel, is to note the people to whom your report was addressed. These are your superiors, correct? First, the military police administration in Ljubuski; second, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command; and third, the assistant chief of military police administration?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And given the witness's answer, Mr. President, to that, we just draw the Court's attention to tabs 6 and 7 of this exhibit which are along the same lines, tab 7 being a communique. If you just turn to tab 7, sir, it's a communique that's issued apparently or ostensibly by the information office of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and it makes reference, amongst other things, to the proclamation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna on page 1, and to the pronouncement of sentences upon two people, two Croats suspected of aggravated robbery and two other Croats suspected of aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about this communique, Colonel, or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours. It's rather illegible, so I need some time to study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't think that we need to spend too much time on this, Colonel. The only point that I wanted to make was that criminal investigations were being performed, cases were being tried, and sentences were being handed out, even under the difficult conditions of wartime and encirclement and siege, essentially, that you faced in the Novi Travnik-Vitez-Busovaca pocket; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. We can move on. You were shown a document by the Prosecution, Exhibit Z1380.2, which was a report dated --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have a copy here for the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is a report, Colonel, that you said was signed by your deputy, Vladimir Santic, and just a list of people in the military police. A couple of questions about this. If you turn to the last page, there appears to be a handwritten request by Colonel Blaskic to follow up on providing another document that identifies how many of the people listed are in commanding positions and to outline the command structure. Do you recall whether you ever did that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not remember, but I think I must have done it, but I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's all right, sir. Now, there are 483 people listed on this list. How many military policemen or military police did you actually have under your control, sir? Was it 483 or some other number?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the structure changed. There was a time when I had, I think, 647 military policemen, and according to the book signed by the minister, the 4th Battalion could have a little over 700 policemen altogether, together with command. But in 1994, I had the highest number of policemen, about 650, on the area controlled by the 4th Battalion. The list changed all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And of these 483 policemen under your command, apparently 5 were assigned to protect Mr. Kordic. If you take a look at page 5 of the Croatian version, it lists Messrs. Santic, Arapovic, Cosic, Lastro and Lovric; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These people appeared on the payroll. Were they actually military policemen or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the situation I found in the 4th Battalion: They were on the payroll only, but their duty was to guard Mr. Kordic. They were to escort him and to be his security guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, just one question about Mr. Kordic. There's no question, sir, that he was never the chief of the HVO Main Staff; you would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the first time I've heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And if you would just turn to page 5, it says, at least according to the translation, "Personal security of the chief of the HVO Main Staff, Colonel Dario Kordic." That was just an error by your subordinate; would you agree with that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm through with that document. And I would just like to ask you a few general questions about your deputy commander, Vladimir Santic. We know that he was actually fulfilling the functions of acting commander of the 4th Battalion of Military Police for some 15 days, I believe you said, prior to your appointment on August 1st of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he remained your deputy commander from August 1st of 1993 until what time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Vlado Santic remained my deputy until the moment when he submitted a request to return to the civilian police, because before the war he used to be a civilian policeman, and throughout the time he was in the military police he was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And could you just -- I just forgot. Could you give us an idea of how long he remained your deputy? From August 1st of 1993 until approximately what time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know, but I know that in 1994, maybe early 1995, he went to the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So we can agree that he was your deputy commander for at least a year and probably more?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you interacted with your deputy on a daily basis; you spoke to him every day, met with him every day during the conduct of your activities as commander. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I had time, I had briefings for my assistants every morning, and then I would go to Colonel Blaskic's regular briefings, because I had to know what the situation was in my 4th Battalion in order to be able to report to Colonel Blaskic. So we did see each other every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so you spoke to and with your deputy commander every day for over a year and a half; you would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, did this deputy commander of yours ever once condemn to you the Ahmici operation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, did this individual who was your deputy commander ever condemn the operation when speaking to his subordinate police officers, to your knowledge? Did you ever hear anything along those lines, ever once?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did your deputy commander ever mention where he had been on the day that the Ahmici killings occurred, April the 16th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never talked about Ahmici with Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so your deputy commander, I take it, sir, never told you that he was actually in Ahmici on April 16th, seen by a woman whose husband he and others murdered?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No. No. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever note, sir, that your deputy commander had any problems in exercising command, any reluctance to do that, any lack of personal courage, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left Vlado Santic as my deputy because, when I arrived, when I took up the post of commander, he told me -- and he behaved very properly -- he told me that he had performed that duty for 15 days, and he wished me good luck, he offered to be there for me in every way and to support me if I needed it. And I knew he had been a civilian policeman and that he was a professional in his job, and that was why I kept him on as my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But did you ever notice any lack of courage or timorousness on the part of your deputy commander when it came to participation in combat operations, or actually -- well, let's leave the question at that. Did you ever notice any of those qualities, lack of courage or timorousness on the part of your deputy commander in exercising his duties as a subordinate commander of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Vlado Santic, throughout the time I was the commander, worked in the command, doing operative tasks. He spent more time in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. He was never perceived as any kind of a personal coward, was he, by the people that he commanded, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. He performed the tasks I gave him. I can't say whether he is a coward or not, but he did his job in a professional manner. I always knew what he was doing, how he was doing it, how far he had got. He always kept me informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the fact of the matter is that he was your second in command and he exercised his command functions without hesitation and without difficulty, as far as you could see; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank God, yes, because otherwise he would not have been in the 4th Battalion, would I have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Now, did he ever profess to you to be suffering from psychiatric or psychological disturbances of any variety at all?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Vlado Santic, he had a kidney complaint, and I know that he was suffering for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... physical problems. I'm interested in mental and psychiatric or psychological problems. Did he ever profess to be suffering from any kind of pangs of guilt, pangs of conscience, any kinds of psychiatric conditions or anything like that to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I -- he never told me, me or in the command, because I would have known the reactions of my other subordinates, so I mean I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it that since he never spoke to you about Ahmici, he never expressed any remorse, misgiving, or concern at any point for the role that he played during the fighting that occurred in mid-April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever notice your Deputy Commander crying every day, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And one final question about your Deputy Commander, you both obviously speak Croatian as your native language, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't notice your Deputy Commander having the slightest difficulty expressing himself in his own language, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sounds like a silly question, but there is an answer; there is a reason for asking the question, Colonel. The question is this: You never noticed your Deputy Commander having the slightest difficulty expressing himself in his native language to you or to the soldiers under his command or to anybody else at any time; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't understand the answer quite. Colonel Palavra, are you answering in the affirmative? Are you saying -- are you confirming what has been suggested by Mr. Sayers? If I understood, your assistant had difficulties in expressing himself in the language which is, which is yours and his? I didn't quite understand that answer. Could you please explain what this is about, because I'm afraid I lost you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry if my question was unclear. I simply wanted the Colonel to agree, and I appreciate that it may at this particular stage appear to be a very silly question, but I wanted him to agree that Croatian was the native language of his Deputy Commander, that his Deputy Commander could speak it, and he never exhibited the slightest difficulty in communicating to others, to his commander, to the soldiers under his command, or to anybody else in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that is true, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. Yes, it is. That is how I understood your question, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope that the reason for that question will become apparent on November the 28th. I wonder if the usher would show the witness Exhibit Z1318A about which he was asked a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions about this document, sir. If you look at this document, it appears to be an order. The Croatian version, at least the cover memorandum, appears to be signed by someone, and it appears to have a stamp. Do you know in fact whether that is the signature of Ivica Lucic? Do you recognise the signature, or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not communicate with Ivica Lucic, but I -- yes, I do think that this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, he purportedly sends along "one item of information," and that's attached to his cover memorandum. Now, can you tell who wrote that? Just to wrap this up, Colonel, there's no way to tell who wrote that excerpt that's attached to -- the item of information that's attached to Colonel Lucic's cover memo, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say, Your Honours, somebody wrote this information, that is, gave it to the chief Ivica Lucic, and on the basis of what he received, he then sent it on to Biskic, that is, the security sector. I don't know who wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, if you just take a look at the stamp next to Ivica Lucic's signature, it says, "Hrvatska Zajednica Herceg-Bosna," the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And indeed, that document, the cover memorandum, appears to be on letterhead that also says "Hrvatska Zajednicz Herceg-Bosna." You would agree with that? I mean, we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the date of the document is three months after the founding of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, isn't it? Ivica Lucic's letter appears, if it's real, to be dated November 26th, 1993, sir -- his cover memorandum, not a letter. But that, you would agree, is three months after the founding of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna and three months after the Croat Community of Herceg Bosna had ceased to exist, yes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you were aware, I believe, sir, that the SIS under Mr. Sliskovic was performing an investigation into what had happened at Ahmici, but, and I think you told this to the Blaskic Trial Chamber at page 16.808, Colonel Blaskic never shared the results of that investigation with you, did he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic never once maintained to you, sir, that local political figures had ordered him to undertake military operations on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. April the 16th, did he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He never mentioned to you that there had supposedly been meetings held on the night of April the 15th between civilian politicians, did he?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. I told you, my task with Colonel Blaskic was to attend morning briefings, naturally be assigned tasks, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you never heard from your daily attendance at the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headquarters and living in Vitez for over -- well, for a few years, you've never heard any contention that attempts were supposedly made to persuade Mr. Kordic to intercede, to stop an imminent attack that was to be launched by the HVO in the Vitez-Ahmici area on April 16th. You've never heard that once, have you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, just to turn to the relationship between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic for a minute, as far as you were aware, throughout your time as military police commander, these two men were on perfectly cordial terms. Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never once heard, throughout the time that you were there in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, living in Vitez, and actually interfacing with or interrelating with Colonel Blaskic on a daily basis, you never heard of any personal disagreements or tension that existed between Colonel Blaskic on the one hand and Mr. Kordic or Mr. Kostroman on the other, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, no. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did Blaskic -- Colonel Blaskic, forgive me, ever complain to you once, even, about any supposed interference in his command by Mr. Kordic, or any other politician, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard any stories going around about such intense disagreements or any kind of disagreements between Mr. Kordic on the one hand and Colonel Blaskic on the other?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if an anonymously authored document were to state that there were in fact acrimonious and bitter discords and disagreements between Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic, what would you have to say about the factual accuracy of any such anonymous document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would say that I think that that is, that is not true because Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Kordic, what terms they were on they will know best. But we, I mean the commanders, we never had any suspicion. We never even suspected that there were some problems between Blaskic and Kordic. Perhaps there was, but we never noticed anything like that even if there was, but I do not think so because they were together always, and I never saw anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Colonel Palavra, you tell us that your conclusion is that there was no friction between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic because, in particular, they were always together? I'm reading from the transcript. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, when I say "always," well, I -- well, they were often together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please be more specific. What does it mean, "often"? Does that mean that that was common knowledge, or did you often see them working together, being together often?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was common knowledge because they held joint press conferences, for instance, in Busovaca or Vitez or ... I mean, that is my answer. I guess they cooperated. They worked together. How often they met, I don't know, but I know they were at press conferences. They were -- and at times, Mr. Kordic would come to the military district in Vitez, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me follow that. What did you think Mr. Kordic was doing at these press conferences and when he was with Colonel Blaskic? What did you think his role was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time, I thought that Mr. Kordic was man number one in matters political in Central Bosnia, and man number one in matters military was, well, Colonel Blaskic. At that time, I know that, in view of the isolation of the Lasva Valley and the impossibility to deblock the media, we, the Croats in Central Bosnia, received the only information -- the only information accessible to us was from those press conferences held in Busovaca, sometimes in Vitez, or I don't know where. That is, we were completely cut off. We simply could not listen to the news. They were all Muslim news, so that we had no knowledge of what was going on in our areas. And it was those press conferences which I believe were held weekly, and I wanted to watch that and to see what was going on. So that we were, I mean, cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's not surprising, Colonel, I think you'll agree, that Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic would be seen together when they would attend these press conferences each week.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The final topic that I would like to cover with you in your cross-examination, Colonel, is the subject of the SIS centre about which you were asked some questions yesterday and some individuals that you identified. But before I do that, did you ever hear of Mr. Kordic or Mr. Kostroman having serious disputes or disagreements with the civilian HVO leaders in Vitez or Busovaca or Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to some of the names that you were asked about yesterday, the first being Miso Mijic. The fact of the matter is, Colonel, that Mr. Mijic has a long background in drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and he was actually drummed out of SIS by Ivica Lucic as a result of those criminal connections; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know. I know Miso Mijic very well as a man, as a man who was in the Travnik municipality even while he played football in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What can you tell us about his criminal background, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know Mijic, I mean, from Travnik days, at the time when he played football, when he was a member of Travnik club Borac. We played together. And then he left. Since he was a good player, he joined Zeljeznicar football club. And for a while -- he was not there long and then he fell ill, and I believe he was retired; that is, he received a pension from Zeljeznicar football club. However, later on in the war he also received some welfare from the HVO; that is, he presented his former illness. I don't know what channels he used, but he managed to get out some benefits, some fringe benefits and compensation, as if he had fallen ill during the war and due to the war, which is not true. Miso Mijic, at the moment -- that is, as far as I know -- immediately after the judgement of Colonel Blaskic was pronounced, went to -- left for Australia or Canada, I wouldn't know exactly -- with his family, and he seldom came to Central Bosnia. And even when he came, he hid. I know that in 1992, at the time when I was with the military police of the municipal staff in Travnik, that he then held a card of the military police of the Travnik municipal staff, signed by late Ivica Stojak, the commander. He and those like him, Voloder, and not to list others, and certain Muslims, had identical cards issued by late Stojak, and they, pretending they were the special police, broke into some flats in Travnik, regardless of whether they were Serb or Muslim or Croat, and they robbed them of jewellery, of gold, of valuables, of money. I did have a meeting with late Commander Ivica Stojak and I suggested to him to urgently abolish those cards because there was the military police in Travnik and there was no need for them to have such cards, and at that time, Ivica Stojak, the then-commander, promised me that he would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did this man, Mijic, ever have any official function of any type, as far as you're aware, representing any organisation in Central Bosnia prior to the time that he fled to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's no question, sir, that he was not actually involved at any time in military matters, and in fact had been banned from attending any meetings of the military commanders of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and of the military police by Colonel Blaskic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never was meetings [as interpreted]. I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were never informed, I take it, sir, as the head of military police, that this dubious individual was masquerading as the supposed chief of the SIS centre, were you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you ever informed that this man Mijic was masquerading as the putative or the supposed chief of something called the SIS centre in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He posed as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was or he wasn't? Did you ever see any orders from anybody in Mostar that actually gave him that status or title, or any authority, anything of that variety?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You never saw any documents that were generated by this man or by the body that he claimed to represent, the SIS centre, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. With the Court's permission, I'd like to have one final exhibit marked, and this is the last series of questions that I have. This is one of the anonymous documents, Your Honour, that has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, it's almost time for a break. It may be sensible to break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got many more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to say, Mr. President, that I will meet my projection. I would anticipate 20 more minutes of examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break now until --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It just may assist the Court's scheduling if I can just tell the Chamber that it appears that, based on the most current information, Witness AO will not be appearing today or tomorrow, and we expect that the other two witnesses, Mr. Morsink and Mr. Husic, can be taken in short order. So we would expect that, depending on the Cerkez examination, that we could finish the evidence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We'll adjourn now until half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I just point out one translation error? Page 27, line 19, it's been translated to be Colonel Kordic, but my Croatian assistant points out to me that the witness actually said "Mr." Kordic. I wonder if I might ask the usher to put on the ELMO a document dated or purportedly dated February the 8th of 1994. It has the initials "BS" on it, and the identification numbers at the top right-hand corner are L0025001 to 09.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A couple of questions, Colonel Palavra. Could you just review this document briefly and let me know if you've ever seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, you have the wrong -- it should be the first page of the document. It's 001 on the top, right-hand -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of questions for a few minutes in connection with this. The author of this document contends that the SIS centre was set up pursuant to an order dated March the 19th, 1993. Now, have you ever seen such an order from the security administration's chief?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. President, I don't believe that this order has been marked as an exhibit yet, and it hasn't been produced in any of the so-called Zagreb materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The author of this document, sir, makes the contention that differences and lack of understanding in relations between the Vitez military district started from the very first day of the alleged operations of this entity, this SIS centre. Do you know anything about that, any differences of opinion between people who purportedly represented themselves as the SIS centre, Mijic being one of them, as you've said, and Voloder being another? And Colonel Blaskic on the other hand, of course.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know anything about this. All I know is that I, as the commander of the 4th Battalion of military police, cooperated with the Security Service at the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, that's fine. If you take a look on the first page, it continues that the main obstacle to the work of this SIS centre outfit from the very beginning is alleged to have been Ante Sliskovic. Do you know anything about that at all? Do you know whether that's truthful or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I see this piece of information. As regards Ante Sliskovic, I haven't read this. I would like to read it, and then I might be able to say more about it. But as far as I know, as regards the army, Ante Sliskovic was the assistant commander for security, and I cooperated with him. But the SIS centre is unknown to me; I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The only authorised official representing the security and information service of whom you were ever aware throughout your time at the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was Mr. Sliskovic. Isn't that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He had the authority to represent the security and information service and, as far as you know, the people claiming to be representatives of this SIS centre outfit did not. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the bottom of page 1, the author of this document contends that Mr. Sliskovic took the position that this SIS centre body was a paramilitary and illegal formation. Have you ever seen any documents ever, sir, that establish that the SIS centre, or so-called SIS centre, was a legal body, that it had any kind of duly delegated authority from any body that had the ability to give that authority?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. The person who authored this document also contends that these SIS centre quasi-operatives, if I may describe them that way, apparently had clashes with not only the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command, Colonel Blaskic, but the top political officials as well. And if we go over to page 2, Mr. Usher, it says that these people had attempted to gain control over the SIS centre. Do you know of any facts whatsoever, sir, that would tend to suggest that that statement is accurate, or not?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So the author goes on to say that because of this obstructionism, or purported obstructionism, on the part of the politicians and the military, then these people, these covert operatives, had to seek the best possible way to function. So what they decided to do was go to the commander of the special purpose unit, the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, and the contention is made that for all practical purposes he is the second most important man in the Vitez Operative Zone. Now, Colonel, that's just not so, is it? Mr. Kraljevic was not in any way the second most important man in the Vitez Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. Kraljevic was not in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone at all. He was the commander of the Vitezovi unit. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the author goes on to say that the SIS centre supposedly started operating in early May of 1993 and that reports and findings and suggestions were submitted to Colonel Blaskic personally, as can be seen, so the author says, "from our files." Have you ever seen any documents, reports, findings, or suggestions that were ever authored by any purported representative of this entity, the SIS centre, that were sent to Colonel Blaskic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, no. I never saw such documents. At least, they were not accessible to me, if there were any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. The document then goes on to describe report numbers, and gives a subject of the reports. And I'm sure if I'm wrong, I'll be corrected, but let me just represent to the Trial Chamber that these documents have not been marked as exhibits and they've not been identified as Zagreb materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, now, what are you asking, Mr. Sayers, that we do with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With this document? I'm just using this document, Your Honour, to -- as an exemplar illustration, if you like, of foundation for similar types of documents, using this witness's personal knowledge as a participant in affairs that this document purportedly describes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but are you asking for the document to be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, not at all. In fact, our position is that this is not a proper exhibit at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, then, I'm not sure on what basis you can possibly refer to it if it's not an exhibit. Either the document is exhibited, in which case you can refer to it, or it's not an exhibit, in which case it's not before the Trial Chamber. I don't think you can have it both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand the point that you make, Mr. President. I don't mind, frankly, having it marked as an exhibit, but I don't want there to be any suggestion on the record that we recognise that this is in any way a real or a valid document or that it actually records events which occurred. We consider this document to be pretty much the product of fiction on the part of people who are trying to evade military service and who were largely involved in criminal activities, as the witness has already said. But we can have it marked as an exhibit if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We take the view that the matter should be exhibited, whatever value it may have or not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have extra copies for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked Defence Exhibit D345/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber's information, we've reached page 3 of the English translation, L0025003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at one of these reports that's mentioned in the top paragraph there, sir. Supposedly there's an order number -- and the document says that, but it's dated October 3rd, 1993, regarding the line of defence at Zaselje. If we go to page 4, the first full paragraph in that page says: "Our operatives have been denied freedom of movement and access either to military units or the lines of defence." Can you tell us, sir, whether you've ever seen any report regarding the line of defence at Zaselje, dated October 3rd, 1993? Does that ring a bell or is that completely foreign to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this piece of information is something I see for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. The next paragraph on page 3 goes on to say that apparently an operative by the name of Adjaip, who I believe is the Boris Adjaip you described yesterday, made a suggestion to Colonel Blaskic, and supposedly Colonel Blaskic made fun of this suggestion and belittled it. What can you tell us about this individual Adjaip? Do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, Adjaip also went to Herzegovina. What he did there, I really don't know, but he left for Herzegovina very quickly and he probably went to the Republic of Croatia. I don't know anything about him except that, when I was in Travnik, he was involved in some sort of logistics, but I don't know exactly what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I'm going to suggest to you, sir, that Mr. Adjaip left the jurisdiction in a serious hurry, along with Mr. Mijic, after the Tuka murder; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What murder?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Zoran Tuka.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They all went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The author of this report then goes on to say that this SIS centre outfit has supposedly submitted 54 written reports to the Vitez Operative Zone command. Once again, I think it's accurate to say that you never saw any such reports, if they were indeed submitted; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, precisely. I didn't see any of those documents, nor was I supposed to see it. If they were sent, then Anto Sliskovic or Colonel Blaskic would know about them. It wasn't my place to know about them. This is the first time I see this information and these documents issued by this SIS service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next contention that is made is that Mr. Sliskovic put Mr. Mirko Selak in the military detention facility at Busovaca in July of 1993. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that Selak was in Kaonik, in Busovaca, but I don't know anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never heard any contention that Mr. Selak, this supposed representative of the SIS centre outfit, was improperly jailed, have you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If we could go over to the next page, page 4, Mr. Usher. The author of this document says that, as I've just recited, the CSIS or SIS centre operatives have supposedly been denied freedom of movement and access to military units or lines of defence. Would you agree with me, sir, that it would be absolutely impossible to write informed reports about lines of defence front lines if you don't go there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in addition, as we've seen from tab 8, I believe, of the exhibits we used with you, sir, Colonel Blaskic refused permission to these people to attend meetings of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command. So there's no way that these people, from personal knowledge, would know of anything that was discussed in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command meetings, the military police discussions, or the discussions of the duly authorised representatives of the security and information service, is there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph on this page makes the observation that these people participated in numerous operations carried out by the Vitezovi. And you've previously told us that, in your view, sir, the people that you've identified, this Mijic, Adjaip, Voloder, these were all people that were operating with Mr. Kraljevic, the commander of the Vitezovi, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, they were even under Kraljevic's protection. I remember in the Security Service after the signing of the ceasefire, a certain amount of weapons were confiscated by Mijic, Voloder, and their men from citizens, allegedly for the needs of the SIS, and they issued receipts, which they signed. So that after the signing of the ceasefire in 1995 and even in 1996, many citizens of Croatian nationality asked for their weapons to be returned to them -- they were hunting rifles, pistols -- because they had properly-signed receipts, signed by Mijic and Voloder, saying that these weapons were being temporarily requisitioned for the needs of the army; but no one ever got their weapon back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The long and the short of it is that this Mijic and Voloder and other CSIS representatives you've identified stole these weapons, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it turned out to be. There has to be some information about what happened to those weapons. Maybe they sold them, I don't know, but people went to the legitimate Security Service with the army, and I saw those documents in the command in the SIS centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Going on, sir, there's a reference on page 5 of the English version of this document to Colonel Blaskic responding to a request for lists of people in the Operative Zone submitted by these SIS centre people, and he basically refused to give them any information about the people under his command, any lists of the people under his command. Were you aware of any such requests being made by these people?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me go to the next page, please. The author then goes on to say that, basically, CSIS was, to a large degree, left to its own devices. And that's the case, isn't it? These people were operating basically without authority and without any official work, as far as you knew; just as sometime members of the Vitezovi sometimes stealing weapons from people?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I have to object. At some point there has to come a limit to the characterisations or arguments of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel, you can answer the question, I think. These people had no authority, they were thieves, they had no officially-defined mission, as far as you knew, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that when the Croats were expelled from Travnik, it was this group that went to the free territory under the control of the HVO. In Travnik, they were in a unit called Rozebrandi, and their status there was also undefined. On their arrival in Vitez, I said I have no idea where they were. I knew they were in hiding and that they asked for protection from the commander of the Vitezovi, that is, Kraljevic, and they were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But the point that I was making is that these people were thieves and, as far as you knew, had absolutely no officially-defined mission in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that they were just acting as sometime members of the Vitezovi, right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it turns out to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. The author of this document also goes on, in the middle of the page, to say that he supposedly received some instructions expounding the place and the role of the CSIS in Central Bosnia in concrete and unambiguous terms. Now, have you ever seen any such instructions, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page, please. I'm going to suggest to you, Colonel, that the next entry throws a lot of light upon what these people were really about. In the middle of the page there, we say -- we see that the observation is made that, being unable to establish professional cooperation with the Vitez Operative Zone, and not having during its entire existence received any kind of assistance by way of fuel or things like that, the CSIS proceeded to steal electric power or to connect illegally the electric power, and then deliberately to keep their premises dim so the police wouldn't find out about it and disconnect it. Now, were you ever aware that power was being diverted along these lines, and these people were trying to stop the police from finding out about it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time I hear this. There's no reason, because they had enough time to clear this up. And Mr. Kordic would know about this, and Mr. Valenta would know about this, and Colonel Blaskic would know about this. They could have solved this at a higher level. All this about the SIS centre, I don't know any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to the next page, there's an incident that's described that supposedly involves you, Colonel.
