This incident occurred on the 19th of December, 1993, and the allegation is made that some of these SIS centre people turned up at a helicopter landing site in Bucici, hoping to transport some computer equipment and other material, and that when they arrived at the landing site, Colonel Blaskic's personal bodyguards opened fire on them. And then you supposedly prevented them from being present when the helicopter landed. Is there -- can you throw any light on that incident, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my task was -- that I had also the order of Colonel Blaskic to -- only those persons who were on the list for the party for Central Bosnia, that is, to allow only those persons who were on the list for the party for Central Bosnia, to allow them to board the helicopter. And I know that the list contained only the names of wounded and the wounded only, and then it also said, "And if there is room for others," then the next one on the list. Not on a single list did figure Mijic or Voloder or their team. I only -- I saw them only once at Bucici when the helicopter landed, and that very moment I ordered them off. There were allegedly to go in the direction of Herzegovina. And with them they were carrying -- I looked at what it was, it was computers, and at that very moment I ordered that back. So once I turned them back, but they then came again. And I believe that those parcels did leave, but I did not allow them to leave. And I reported to Colonel Blaskic about it, telling him that that should not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The author of this document goes on to say that a computer monitor, supposedly belonging to Boras Adjaip went missing, and that these people supposedly contacted you, and you told them that you had -- that they could sue either the Operative Zone or you personally, whichever suited them. Is there any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can see for yourselves. In this, I am mentioned in this document. I don't know where did Boras Adjaip get a computer or a monitor. I do know at that time at the Princip, that is in Vitez, I mean a company, were they together with Kraljevic and his, his small team where they were stealing computers. And until I turned up at the helicopter, they used to sell them down there in Herzegovina, using what channels I don't know. But it is these computers, and in one case, a computer and a monitor. And when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, this isn't important. It seems to me it is going somewhere from the point. You were going to finish in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm going to finish in one minute, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next comment and final comment is on page 9, sir, where supposedly on January the 1st, 1994, the police received an order to bring in these people and assign them to military duties to the 3rd Battalion of the Viteska Brigade, and then certain other allegations are made after that. Let me just suggest to you that that reveals the truth of the situation. It shows what really is going on, and that these people were thieves and criminals trying to duck military service by pretending to be carrying out some sort of unofficial, covert, civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Some sort of unofficial, covert, civilian spying for a shadowy organisation that had no official function whatsoever in Central Bosnia, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's what it looks like indeed, because when we realised what they were and who they were, then naturally they also had to be assigned to the front lines, like everybody else. That is, they were sent to the front line, where they had never been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Palavra. I am Bozidar Kovacic and I'm counsel for Mario Cerkez. I'm counsel for Mario Cerkez with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. I also have some questions for you. They won't take too long. You said that you came to Vitez after you had to withdraw from Travnik in June 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that, for a short while before you were assigned to a new duty at the military police -- with the military police, that a short while then you spent at the defence line. Could you just briefly indicate the exact locations.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was in the area of responsibility of Travnik Brigade, that is, at Prahulje, up there at Prahulje. I was also -- now, what was that called? Gostinj, so up there. Bosnjakov Gaj. These are the locations where I was, so that was the area of responsibility of the Travnik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, you will agree with me that that area of responsibility was outside the municipal -- Vitez municipal boundaries?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time when you arrived in the Vitez territory, until your assignment, how familiar were you with the situation in Vitez with regard to the structure and other elements of the HVO functioning in Vitez, especially in terms of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not familiar at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So is it then true that when you carried out the duties that you did carry out in Travnik, because you were pushed out of there, you did not have any relevant information about the HVO in general, the HVO in general, and that would include the Vitez Brigade in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Central Bosnia is it correct to say that the HVO began to organise its brigades as of December 1992 onward?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And before that, there were the municipal staffs. You told us about them yourself.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you learn when you arrived in Vitez that the Vitez Brigade, in contrast with almost all other brigades, was founded only as late as the latter half of March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. You do not know the exact date. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that that brigade was founded later than other brigades?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you no doubt know that that was much later in comparison with other brigades?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, prior to that time -- or rather, in July, and then especially in August, when you became the police commander, perhaps in due course you received some information, an idea about the level of structuring of the Vitez Brigade on the day when the conflict broke out between the BH army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you did not hear any stories about how the brigade was at a very low organisational level at the time when the war began?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, not only the Vitez Brigade; all the brigades were at a low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us how in fact you were not in a position to command your companies in Kiseljak and Zepce simply because you were physically cut off from those towns since they were completely encircled and they were practically commanded by local commanders -- I don't know -- Rajic in Kiseljak and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, quite. Since it was impossible to communicate with units of the 2nd Company in Kiseljak and the 3rd Company in Zepce, my subordinate commanders were at the disposal, both at Rajic's and General Lozancic's, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think there is any question about it. After all, you did mention it and we already heard it umpteen times before the Court. So will you please answer only with "yes" or "no." But the commander of the Operative Zone was in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the town itself, the 4th HVO Battalion was also headquartered -- I mean, the 4th Battalion of the Military Police was in Vitez too?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was housed in the police building, with the police administration on the upper floor. Those were the premises of the former Territorial Defence, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the situation also before you came?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, the command of the Vitez Brigade was also in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the Vitez Brigade was also in Vitez, in the Hrvatski Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which is a couple hundred metres from those other locations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is all within 100-, 150-metre circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you -- oh, excuse me. I am being too fast. Would you agree with me, then, that insofar as communication was concerned between different commands, in contrast with the situation that you used to have when the commanders of military police with Kiseljak and Zepce, that in this particular case there was not that problem in communication between the Operative Zone, military police; military police and the Vitez Brigade; the Vitez Brigade and the Operative Zone and the like?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with this. We could do it even if we did not have any telecommunication means. We could do it on foot or with couriers, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in that regard, Vitez was under specifics [as interpreted] because all the commands were located there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned something. There was mention about the brigade military police. Did you, at the time when you became the commander, get any relevant information about a military police platoon attached to the Vitez Brigade to provide security for the buildings and the like? Did you have any information as to how that had been solved by that time, or before your arrival there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't really remember. You know, it was seven years ago. But I know that the brigade platoons of the military police had their specific tasks, and that was to secure the command posts, of the brigades, that is, and to bring in to the brigades people under different disciplinary sections. Those were their powers. And as for the curfew, which was controlled by the military police at the time, that is, the regional one, so all they did do was bring under custody, and the brigade police. Those were their powers: Only bringing in within their own brigade and command posts which they secured. Those were their only terms of reference. All the rest was done by the brigade police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps now is the right time to ask you, since you mention it. Did these duties that you mentioned were the mandate of the brigade police, would it also cover what you call military police affairs?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, some of them. But there are other military police affairs, aren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We didn't get an answer to that question. What does the question in fact mean, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. It must have been my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that those were so-called military police affairs, those that we mentioned: Bringing in soldiers, members of the brigade, and security, providing security, looking after the safety of the command. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So I'm talking in police terms. When you say "providing security for the command," that means the building, the facility housing the command, and personnel?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That was their task. And other military police tasks -- for instance, escorting convoys, manning checkpoints -- that was done by the regional police. The observations of the curfew, that was all done by the regional police. That was not within the authority of the brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Palavra, tell us: Did you have an opportunity to see, because it was all going on before you came there, but did you ever see an order issued by the command of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police which would -- addressing the platoon assigned to staff security there, that that attached formally that platoon to the command of the Vitez Brigade? Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was a long time ago, but I think that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you are not quite sure?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, I cannot really say yes or no. It was just too long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you do not know exactly from your personal experience whether there was such an order?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible that there was, because I know that the brigade police, not only of the Vitez Brigade but of the other brigades as well, communicated with the command of the 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at the time when you became the commander, is it fair to say that there were certain ambiguities, that members of that particular platoon had their own views, under whom they were and who was their commander, that the brigade also had its requests with regard to your command? Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document -- no. Let me ask you this first: Do you remember if you personally asked Blaskic to clarify the situation toward the lines and define who is under whom, who commands whom?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now I will show you a document. I will ask you to comment on it. It is D91/2, order of Colonel Blaskic's of the 18th of August, 1993. Will you have a look at this, please. My question to you is to round off this set of questions and also on the basis of this document. This is at the time when you were already the commander of the regional military police, and you're obviously interested in this subject professionally. Would you agree with me that, as of that day, there were no more problems and it was evident who commanded the brigade police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, not only in Vitez; in all the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean those which were under the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And incidentally, since you mentioned others, were there any similar problems in other brigades as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since those other brigades were in towns which were at some distance, some completely cut off from the Operative Zone, would it be correct to say that this situation was dissolved on a case-by-case basis, depending on the possibilities, in view of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, you will agree that, as regards the membership in formations of the subordination of those platoons of the military police attached to brigades, this situation in Central Bosnia was not necessarily identical from one municipality to the other?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I guess you will agree, in view of what we have just talked about, and especially with regard to the time in the previous period and the later period, that there was a difference?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just add, that as original police, that is, the 4th Military Police Battalion, looked -- provided the brigade, platoons with patches, that is, with military police insignia. They received them from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of what you have just said, does that mean that administratively, in any case administratively, those members, although they were attached at some point, clearly attached to brigade commanders, but administratively, they were under the command of the regional battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite, because at that time, brigades could not issue the military police -- patches to military police, and they got those patches from the 4th Battalion military police, and the 4th Battalion of the military police received them from the police administration with a seat in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that also mean that those military policemen from those platoons, in those platoons, their rights, exercised those rights -- or rather, their payrolls, that they were on the payrolls of the 4th Battalion, in your particular case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And all the training, and all the training that was organised was also -- also involved the brigade police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they issued with weapons and ammunition and other gear, if you remember it, of course?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that many of them were issued with those by the military police, but because the military police lacked them, too, some of them may have been issued with the relevant gear by the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, since you received all sorts of reports, what kind of a stamp did they use when they sent their reports, either to brigade commanders or the 4th Battalion, that is, the commander of the 4th Battalion? Is it true that they had a stamp which showed clearly that they belonged to the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to cut this short, if possible. In addition to military police affairs performed by the military police and that we touched upon, and one can find it in detail in a document that was shown yesterday, Z2340, and I do not wish -- I do not want to waste any more time. This is a document which describes police province, police jurisdiction. Yet you told us about this, that the military police discharged some business of typical military units. You even mentioned, if I'm right, that you intervened in a number of situations when the front line was in peril or when it was broken through, when it fell, and that your units then went at those critical points in order to stop the breakthrough of the adversary forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But these are purely combat activities, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was such an incident when there was a convoy leading to Novi -- on its way to Nova Bila, the so-called Bijeli Put, the white pass. At that time, the Krizancevo Selo was victimised, that is, the Muslim forces had attacked it. And as soon as the convoy had got on, that is, the white pass, the members of the military police did, did not sleep for three nights because that very moment they went out to intervene, that is, stop the Muslim attacks, and they went directly to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The members of your military police in such actions, you personally had to order them to go to such and such location with such and such task; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Who else would do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who did issue orders to you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Colonel Blaskic who issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, was Mario Cerkez authorised to issue such orders?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not only Mario Cerkez, but no brigade -- or rather, every brigade commander had to seek authority of Colonel Blaskic, and only Colonel Blaskic would then transmit to me whatever was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I suppose -- yes, I see that I'm too fast. I suppose that you must remember some of the situations when the brigade commander asked for some assistance in order to, in order to save a part of the front line, and that requested assistance from you, and that Colonel Blaskic asked it from you. Is that correct? You don't have to give us examples.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it also possible that, in some emergency, you acted on the direct order of Mario Cerkez's?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There would always be somebody from the Operative Zone, whether the chief or Colonel Blaskic or the duty -- the operations officer on duty, somebody had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In point of fact, according to some information available to us, you took great care, very meticulously, that there be an order, a very precise order determining the area, the task, and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I cannot do something which is vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you at any moment -- or rather, you said at a moment that Blaskic could not have ordered an investigation into criminal offences. Do you think Cerkez could have done so? Do you think Cerkez's authority was different from that of Blaskic in that realm?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Palavra, let me ask you first, you had an assistant besides the Santic who we have mentioned. I think we also mentioned Jukic, a pre-war policeman, who knew -- who was familiar with the law and criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Marijan Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the department Jukic was in was engaged in criminal prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the crime military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As the commander, were you familiar with the fact that every citizen under the then legislation adopted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian community as well, that under the then valid legislation, every citizen, or every soldier in this case, including the brigade commander, could submit a criminal report if he knew that a crime had been committed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And such a criminal report in the case of Vitez would have been submitted to your crime service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then this service would have sent it on to the military prosecutor's office at that time if there were indications or grounds to suspect, and that a report had to be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To avoid any misunderstanding, if a report was received from anyone, any citizen, including Cerkez, your crime detection service would have looked at the evidence, clues, traces, and so on, and processed these; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in any case, would have submitted a report to the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The military public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did that on a weekly and monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, the military prosecutor's office as an organ under the law functioned in Vitez. You mentioned Mr. Mario Jurkovic a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course, in the given circumstances as far as was possible?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the military court existed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there were cases where proceedings were instituted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the approximate number of criminal reports submitted by your service from August 1993 until the end of 1993 to the public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember, but I know that certainly there were over 500. I don't know the exact number. I think it was about 546, perhaps, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Palavra, in any case, we are talking about several hundred and not several dozen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When we say "submitted to the public prosecutor," for the sake of the record, we are referring to the military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the military prosecutor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your service processing criminal reports, when a criminal offence was reported to you, that you processed every report you received from anyone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you also received such reports from the brigade command, either through their reports on incidents or through especially written reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. There were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, let me mention a document Z1245.4 that was presented yesterday. It was a report from the 2nd Vitez Battalion, and you said that it referred to, among other things, the car thefts, and you said that Anto Furundzija had been punished for it; is that correct? And my question is the following: Was that incident treated as a disciplinary infraction or as a criminal offence; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was both a disciplinary infraction, but also a report was submitted against Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Palavra, during your work in Vitez from the summer of 1993 onwards, did you have occasion to meet Mario Cerkez and to get to know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. We met at the regular meetings on Fridays or Thursdays, or whenever Colonel Blaskic convened the meeting, and when I took over the duty of commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, I visited all the commanders of the brigades on the -- in the area of Central Bosnia, in Vitez and Novi Travnik and the part of Travnik and in Busovaca. I think that on two or three occasions, I talked to Mario Cerkez, who was the commander of the Vitez Brigade, about the status of the military police and what should be done further to, to avoid any disagreements. I have to admit that he received me very politely and supported me in everything I said. He agreed with my ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Palavra, you have talked a lot about Vitez, about crime there. Would you agree that in Vitez there was in fact a structure that was interested in order and discipline, and this included both civilians and soldiers, people of importance; but that there was also another group which we could call either close to crime or criminals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct because the area of Vitez, unfortunately, after the attack of the Muslim forces on Zenica, Travnik, Kakanj, and Fojnica, many refugees arrived in the area of the Vitez municipality which was under HVO control, and there were all kinds of things going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Palavra, in your opinion, throughout this time that you knew Cerkez and all the problems you had in the second half of 1993 in Vitez, where would you put Cerkez, into which of these two groups, in the first or the second group, or somewhere in between? Can you say that, because you knew what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, had Mario Cerkez been different from what he was, he would probably not have been the commander of the Vitez Brigade because I know Colonel Blaskic well, and he would not have allowed it. Cerkez was respected in Vitez, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Colonel Palavra, did you ever hear any rumours to the effect that Cerkez or his men had committed any war crimes, any kind of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's a ridiculous question. No, no. Why would they commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, if the Court will allow, I can put a simple question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday there was a question about a certain Mr. Mato Zeko, and you spoke about him, but I'm not interested in him, I'm interested in something else. Was that the only person of the same name and surname that you knew? Was there anyone else with the same name and surname in the area where you lived and worked?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honours, the name of Mato and the surname of Zeko belonged to one, single individual that I know of. There is, however, someone called Ivica Zeko. So the first name is "Ivica" and the last name "Zeko." That person also exists, and during the wartime events in Central Bosnia, that person is now in the Ministry of Defence of the army of the federation, that's Ivica Zeko. But the only Mato Zeko I know is that one. There may be others, but I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this Ivica Zeko that you mentioned was, if I'm correct, the assistant for VOS affairs with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The assistants that you mentioned earlier at the level of the brigade command, the brigade commander had several assistants; is that correct? You knew that. And he had, among others, an assistant for SIS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you in fact met the late Borislav Josic, who was killed soon after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I never met him, but I have heard about him. I have heard a lot of good things about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A lot of good things?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The assistant for SIS, according to his function, would you agree that his basic task was to inform his commander, in this case the brigade commander, to keep him informed about everything?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see I'm talking too fast. Is it correct that, according to his function, this assistant would have another boss?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and that would be the assistant for security at the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia at the time, and that was Ante Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Colonel, that if the assistant, in this case the assistant for SIS, contacted you, you would not know whether he was acting on behalf of the brigade commander or on behalf of his other superior in the functional line?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was not clear enough. The assistant for SIS, for example, he comes to you with a request, and you do not necessarily know whether he is asking this as the subordinate of the brigade commander or as the subordinate in this other line, as the assistant in the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the criterion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criterion was I could be contacted by the assistant for the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could he have authorised his colleague in the brigade to do something on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would have known about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was my question. So you would have had to have been informed about this?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more detail and I will be finished. I would like to make use of your presence here. I know that you have on average about 600 men under your command, so you couldn't have known them all, but do you remember in the military police units in Vitez a person named Ivica Markovic from Kotor Varos who was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO PALAVRA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know. There was a Markovic who worked in the crime detection service, but I think he was in Zenica. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Maybe you can assist us while you are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a person who was mentioned by the first witnesses who testified here who were arrested in town and taken to the SDK, so I thought maybe we could see if it was the same person, but evidently this witness doesn't know. I have no further questions. Thank you, Colonel Palavra. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Palavra, that concludes the questions you're going to be asked. I said at the outset that if there was anything you wanted to add, we would hear you. We will do so. You don't have to add anything, of course, and only deal with the relevant matters. If there is anything relevant you would like to add, we'll hear it, or otherwise you're free to go. Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for coming, Colonel Palavra. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might just raise one issue, Your Honour. The batting order and witness statements, we don't have a definitive batting order for the witnesses who are going to be testifying next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's one of the matters we've got to resolve in the next day. Mr. Scott, which witnesses have you got here now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we're prepared, Your Honour, to put Mr. Morsink and Mr. Husic on this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We should be able to deal with them without too much difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right, and that would be it for the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that would be it for the week. We will then have to consider next week which witnesses, first of all, are to be called. You should let the Defence and also the Court know as soon as possible, like this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think this afternoon, probably, if we don't -- presumably we don't have court tomorrow, then we would let the Chamber know this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see. I anticipate we'll sit this afternoon, this afternoon and tomorrow, in order to try and deal with the Zagreb documents. If that is so, it means that we can advance all the proceedings for the remainder of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The only problem, Your Honour, as Mr. Nice mentioned earlier in the week, is that, to be perfectly honest, although we've tried to accelerate our preparations, much of our schedule is still hinged on certain matters being done on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us -- we'll review that this afternoon, but we have in mind to accelerate things in order that we can get the Defence rejoinder evidence in, and the speeches, by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can only tell the Court that some of the materials might not be ready by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see how we go. We'll sit again at half past two o'clock. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.51 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I gather there's something you wanted to raise before we get to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, if I may. It doesn't concern the witness or his evidence at all. The documents that fall for consideration next week were, of course, provided to the Defence a couple of weeks ago. In the intervening weeks the Court wasn't sitting, I inquired via your legal officer whether the Court would itself want copies of the documents or whether it would at that stage want any schedules, and no request for the documents was made, and therefore they haven't been copied. It's quite a big exercise to copy three bundles and add to the weight of paper. But it occurs to me as possible that the Chamber would probably or might benefit by having not just schedules, which can be in final form, I think, this afternoon or certainly tomorrow morning, but might benefit from having the opportunity to look at the documents ahead of next week's hearings. If so, then I'll trigger their copying straight away, and then they might be available -- in fact, I think they could probably be available for the Court tomorrow morning. And I understand the Court was concerned as to how tomorrow morning could be used, and that is at least one way in which it might be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will, after we've heard the evidence today, need to look at all the housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But yes, I think copies would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay, I'll get that done, then, straight away. Thank you for allowing me to raise that. And then I think the witness should probably take the solemn declaration again, but he's probably bound by the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's bound by the first one he took; no need to take it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think, technically, the position is that the only exhibit for which we wanted to recall is now already in by virtue of the formal statement, subject to the right of Mr. Kovacic for cross-examination. So I don't think there's anything for me to deal with because the exhibit is now in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Morsink, thank you for coming back. There is, I'm afraid, one matter of evidence outstanding which was overlooked on the first occasion when you gave evidence. It's in relation to a list of detainees. It is our Exhibit Z591, [transcript read in error"7591], not that you're troubled with that, but one counsel has asked to ask you some questions about it, and we've allowed him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, of course, you are, as you know, restricted to simply this issue, 591, the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if the witness had the exhibit, so you knew what we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, could it also be put on the ELMO or could the interpreters get copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the interpreters haven't got a copy. Is there a copy to be put on the ELMO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, I don't know if you remember that list.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I do remember it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it may have your writing on it.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could begin, since it's in Dutch, if you would translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: The translation is, "The list of Muslims being taken prisoner by the HVO Vitez."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just for a matter of record, I don't know whether it was the error, but the number of this exhibit was mentioned, 7591. It is actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Zeta, Zeta 591, or zee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then it is correct so we have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel Morsink. I do apologise for making you come again, but we have a document which you supplied to the Prosecution at a later stage; we thought we should ask you some questions about it. Last time, during your testimony here, you used some notes as an aid. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I do remember it, but I brought them with me, the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are not using them now, are you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: As long as I don't have to need -- use them, I'd rather do it on the basis of my memory, if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we shall talk only about this list. You made your solemn declaration. We already saw it. You attached the list to it. Now, do you confirm that the list that you have before you is the list which you personally handed over to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, and who did you get this list from?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I got this list from the HVO representative, the liaison officer, Borislav Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- no. It seems that I have to wait for the interpreters. Could you perhaps roughly specify when you received it from Borislav Jozic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I can't exactly specify the date, but it was somewhere in the end of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we relate it perhaps to some events? Would you know if it was at the time while there were still some detained Muslims in Vitez, or was it after their release?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: As I recall it, there were still quite a lot of people in prisons on both sides, and we were busy trying to get a clear picture of prisoners in all prisons, and this list is part of our attempt to get a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was doubtless at the time when a commission, who Jozic was a member of the commission for ceasefire, exchange of prisoners, and so on and so forth, that commission had already been founded and was already working; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: As I recall it, it was more or less in the time that we switched from the Busovaca joint commission on to the new established local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you specify if at the time when the late Boro Jozic gave you this list, had you already -- was it after some other meetings with Boro Jozic and other members of the commission? That is, did you know at that moment that he was already on that commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the local commission where I was -- the commission I was heading and there was also a representative from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that commission.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Part of every day's discussion was, amongst other things, the situation of prisoners in the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, would you agree that there is absolutely no doubt that your communication with the late Boro Jozic -- and you tell us that he gave you this list -- that your communication is based on the fact that you know him; he was introduced to you as a member of the commission on behalf of the Croat side, that is, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to really be on the safe side, I should like to ask the engineers to show a tape. It is our early Exhibit 118/2, adduced with witness Palavra, and it contains a short statement by Mr. Jozic to a television reporter. It does not take -- we shall only show the first part of it, and it is only a minute and 16 seconds. Could the technical booth please show us the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We can stop here now. Could we only have the image on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Morsink, do you recognise this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise him as Mr. Borislav Jozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is the person who gave you the list?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We do not need the tape anymore. Could the registry please give the witness the transcript of the video. Perhaps we can put it on the ELMO so that everybody can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So I'd like to draw your attention to the first paragraph in the answer of Borislav Jozic. So the first paragraph is the journalist and the second one is the answer. And here he says -- the text is in English, so everybody can read it. Colonel Morsink, do you agree with the -- what is said in the first passage of this statement? Do you agree that this first paragraph in the statement -- the rest is not, I think, as important -- is that correct, that first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: You mean the introduction by the journalist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no. I mean the answer, the first passage, the first paragraph of Mr. Jozic's answer.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is correct, right? Now, if you look at the next paragraph, will you please read it? I'm sorry. Perhaps I'm wasting your time, but I think it is very important, especially the sentence in the middle, which refers to location. Colonel Morsink, do you agree that it transpires from this statement by the late Borislav Jozic, with regard to the event that he's talking about, deals with the release of prisoners from one of the locations that were mentioned, and that is the location in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I'll read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me get it straight. Yes. The question is -- is this the question, that Jozic was talking about the release of prisoners from Dubravica? Yes, that's what -- you didn't ask the witness. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my idea was to see whether the witness could recognise, since there were a couple of locations, and he said in original statement that he knew there were a couple of locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it you want the witness to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I will show the witness the list of Dubravica detainees, and we shall compare it with his list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why don't you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I nevertheless would like to seek an answer to my question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, do you remember that detainees were kept at several locations in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct; in Vitez and outside the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the school in Dubravica was one of those locations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the only location where detainees were kept in the building of the school was precisely this one in Dubravica, that there is no other school which was used as a place of detention?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I can't tell about other towns or vicinities. I think Dubravica is that small that I agree that this is probably the only school in Dubravica, but there were certainly more schools in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're referring to the area of Vitez. Dubravica is a part of Vitez. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry then help me distribute the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And while it is being distributed, perhaps I could ask you the following, Colonel Morsink: Do you know anything from that list that was given you who are these individuals? What is their status? Are they civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but by the name, I can tell you that they are probably only male prisoners; and by the age or the year of birth, I can tell you that the age is somewhere between 16 and I think 75 or 77.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with us that an overwhelming majority are of military age, able-bodied men, judging by their date of birth. Do you agree with that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think the majority of this list, that's correct, that's an age that could mean that they can be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, you have before you a list of members of the BiH army from the municipality of Vitez. This list was given the Defence by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina at our request, and on lists -- there it lists some -- features 3.623 names who, during the war, were members of the BiH army and served at some point in time in that army. Now I should like to ask you to look at your list, the list that you brought along, and look at the name under "1." It is a certain individual named Hajrudin Zisko, son of Mehmet. Have you found it, number one?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's hard to read on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mine is slightly better. You can see it, at any rate. This is a regular exhibit. Now, take this roster of the army, the big one, and turn to the last page. The big one, yes, and turn to the last page. In the first column, you have numbers, and then will you look at a person under 3613, 3613, Hajrudin Zisko. We also have the personal identity number showing us the date of birth, and that is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: The name is the same, and the date is also the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the father's name. Now, we can show other such examples. For instance -- do you have the BiH army's list? Yes, you do. Look at number 59, please, on the first page of the army list, Dervis Jahija Ahmic, we again have the personal identity number with the date of birth, and you will find him, too. That's a person under number four of the list that you brought, also on your page number one, under number four.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's again the same name and the same date as on the army's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Same father's name and same date of birth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. I can quote, however, ordinal numbers in Mr. Morsink's list, for instance, example 7, 8, 11, and there are some others. There is no point in wasting time. I think the documents speak for themselves. But there's the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before we go on, let us get the status of these documents. Is there any objection to the production of this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think I've ever seen it before, and I don't know where it comes from, and I'm not sure what its purpose is at the moment. If it's going to do no more than confirm that which the Colonel has already said, namely, that many of the people on this list of his were soldiers, it doesn't seem to me it takes matters very much further. If the inverse exercise is being attempted, that is to say, if the reality is that Mr. Kovacic is seeking by cross-examination to validate this list, it seems to be an improper use of the witness and if he'd asked me about it, I would probably have been able to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't anticipate that he's seeking to do that. For the moment, let it have an exhibit number, and if there's some objection, we can look at it again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered D153/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, no doubt you've been through these two lists. Can you give us the total number that you say appear from the army list on the present list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honours, not yet. We're still at it. I found 30 something, but evidently there are more of them. We have some problems with reading them, but we've fed it into the computer the other day, and we are preparing a longer list. But we shall enclose it with the documentation. However, now I should also like to adduce two more documents which will help, help us establish the authenticity of the list. No, one document, sorry. I do not think that the witness can validate the list. This is only for the Court and for my learned friend. It is a letter of the Bosnia-Herzegovina embassy, sending this list to me, and evidently this is being done at my request. I do have some early copies of that correspondence. Could it then be merely attached to this exhibit just as part of the exhibit, or perhaps it should be given another number, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be simpler to have another number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I should like to produce yet another list and ask Colonel Morsink to look at it after he confirmed to us that there were detainees in Dubravica. I'm sorry, I mixed things up. Will you please leave the list of Dubravica names with Colonel -- the list of the BiH army and 153/2; the witness should have all those lists, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Last document will be numbered D155/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go any further, what is this document, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we do not have the translation of this document, but all that needs to be translated is the first line, and I will read it in Croatian and the interpreters can interpret it. Oh, no, excuse me, we do have the translation. This is a list of persons detained in Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where did you get this one from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it myself in Vitez sometime in the beginning of 1998, in the early days of our investigation. My only question -- I have only two questions to ask the witness about this list. May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you ever get this list from anyone from the HVO or the BiH army while you worked on the commission that we mentioned a while ago? Does it look familiar to you, that is what I'm trying to ask you. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have just discovered a typing error. The date of that list should be 30 April, not April 4 on the translation. On the original, of course, it is original?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I saw this list before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is -- there is an objective possibility for this list to include some of the same names that we saw on the list of the BiH army, and that those same names figure on this list of detainees in Dubravica? I'll show you. For instance, this last list that we've given you, persons detained in Dubravica, under "3" we have Smajo Avdic, son of Mujo, born in 1942, and that same person figures also in this list of BiH army members on page 3, ordinal number 183.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It looks like the same name to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let us take yet another example. In this Dubravica list, individual under "5," Hasan Sipcic, and in this list of BiH army soldiers is on page 37 under "2922."

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: It again looks like the same name to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then also person under "7."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honours, that there is really no need to go through this whole list, because there are quite a number of them and we shall refer to this in our closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you all these questions, Colonel Morsink, let us go back to your list. Do you know -- did Jozic tell you anything that these 299 persons are a list of people detained in one location or several locations? What does this list represent? Of course, it refers to detained persons, but from where? Did Jozic tell you anything about this?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I do not recall that he told me specifically to what location this list referred. He was more or less responsible to, to make lists of the whole Vitez area, and I do not recall whether he told me that this list referred to only one specific location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Morsink, it seems to me that it follows from your testimony, and please correct me if I'm wrong, that the Dubravica location was controlled by the Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I recall that you asked me that before, and if I'm correct, I answered that I recall that and I still recall that, that the guardsmen were wearing special insignia on the shoulders, and according to those insignia, they were members of military police. I can't say whether this was the Vitezovi unit or any other military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, were you able to distinguish HVO units by uniform, units within the HVO, who were the military police, the Vitezovi, the Cerko [phoen] Brigade, the Vitez Brigade? Did you know about it? Did you have enough knowledge of it at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Certainly not enough knowledge to identify them all, but I was aware who was supposed to be a military policeman and who not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the cross-examination was supposed to refer to this list. We went through all these other matters before. There is other evidence about it, and I don't think we should detain the Colonel for this sort of cross-examination. Have you got anything else you want to ask about the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only two or three technical matters related to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, can you remember where Boro Jozic gave you the list, in what location and what place, especially in what place? Was it at a meeting or while you were going around the terrain or in Dubravica when you were there?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: Normally, we got these lists from both sides when they were prepared during the morning meeting at the ECMM house near the BritBat battalion base. So there was our own ECMM house in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one more question. At these meetings where these lists were often presented, Boro Jozic was always present exclusively as a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you -- what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Boro Jozic was present at that meeting as one of the members, not as an observer or a guest who happened to be there or someone whose role was simply to bring along a piece of paper. His function was that he was a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was the liaison officer assigned by the brigade commander of the HVO brigade in Vitez, so he was representing -- at least, that was my impression -- representing the HVO brigade in Vitez during all these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him explicitly whether he was representing the whole of the HVO in Vitez, the HVO Operative Zone under Blaskic's command? You knew -- well, let us divide this question in parts. You knew that he was an officer from the Vitez brigade; is that correct? There is no doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever formally establish whose representative -- I apologise to the interpreters. Did you ever, for the sake of the minutes, try to establish that Boro Jozic, and that is what I am suggesting to you, at those meetings was a representative of the Operative Zone? I will ask just one more question about this and then I'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, he was only representing the brigade, since Mr. Cerkez wrote a letter of accommodation to appoint him as his representative, the same as the BiH side did, and on the level of the HVO Operational Zone we had a special liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But not a member of the commission; you did not have a member of the commission at the level of the Operational Zone. The only representative on the HVO side was Boro Jozic; do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: For Vitez matters, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We are talking about Vitez matters. So the only representative for Vitez matters on behalf of the HVO, the entire HVO side, without any distinctions, was Boro Jozic; there were no other representatives of the HVO present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's not fully correct, since during some occasions the brigade commander, accompanied by some other officers, showed up himself, so it's not always only Mr. Jozic. But I do not recall another individual being a representative for the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Morsink, let us draw a distinction between two things: One were the meetings and the other was the commission. You talked about the work of the commission, so we were talking about the meetings referring to the work of the commission, not all the other meetings. So as a member of the commission, the only one on the HVO -- on behalf of the HVO was Boro Jozic, and the documents show this. Do you hold a different opinion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't agree that you can make a clear distinction between the work of the commission and meeting brigade commanders. We had to do a lot of work on the ground in the whole area and we met brigade commanders several times, twice or three times a day. It was also the work of the commission. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we've already exhausted this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think I understand the point. [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you for your testimony. Thank you, Colonel Morsink.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything I need raise with the colonel, and I have no objection to the documents going in that have been produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming back to give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the next witness will be Mr. Husic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- who is coming back to deal with the tape, he having been the witness who produced it. And there were some matters you wanted to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. He's been brought back for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, for cross-examination. But I mean, essentially, it's your point that if this tape -- if it's being suggested that this tape has been interfered with and manipulated, then it should be put firmly to the witness who is responsible or may have been responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Precisely, yes. The only thing that may need explaining, not by me, perhaps, but to the witness, is, of course, that on the previous occasion he was cross-examined by Mr. Stein, and so it will be somebody else, in case he notices these things. Yes, that's the position there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you agree with that point, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do, but it's going to be Mr. Naumovski that does the cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I think the witness is bound by his previous taking of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Husic, there's no need to take that again. You've already taken a declaration to tell the truth and you are, of course, still bound by it. If you'd like to take a seat. The position, Mr. Husic, is this: You've been asked to come back because various other issues about the tape which you produced have been aired during the course of evidence since you last gave evidence, and it is thought right that you should have the opportunity to deal with any suggestions which may be made about the authenticity of the tape. You're going to be cross-examined by counsel, different counsel, but representing the same accused. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My name is Mitko Naumovski. I am an attorney at law from Zagreb and I am the defence counsel for Mr. Kordic, together with Mr. Sayers. Since we understand each other as soon as we speak, please wait a little for my question to be interpreted into the official languages of the Tribunal so as not to make the work of the interpreters more difficult. Mr. Husic, you made a statement to investigators of the Tribunal on the 4th of December, 1999. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: After that, you testified before this Court in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I assume that yesterday, or in recent days, you looked at your testimony from the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you read your previous statement of the 4th of December, 1999?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, whether you also read the testimony of the expert witnesses, Messrs. Kanik [phoen] and others who testified after your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And have you discussed their expert opinion with anyone at all?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And just one more question for the sake of clarification. You know nothing of what the experts found?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: What I know is that, when I testified here for the first time, I was told that two tapes which I handed over were completely identical. That's all I know. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Then we will not go into this further. Tell us, please: In the meantime, did you have a meeting with the Prosecutor or investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor from the time of your last testimony up to the present moment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I had contact with them yesterday because I was sitting down and reading those materials, and I had contact with Mr. Patrick Lopez-Terres, and I asked him why I had been called here again and he told me that he assumed I was here so that it could be established again, so to say, to establish the identity or to identify this material, if you call that a meeting, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, my question would be: Apart from this information as to why you were here, did you discuss with him or anyone else the content of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please: Did you, in the meantime, have any contacts or any conversation with Adnan Begovic or (redacted) ? I assume you know who I'm referring to. These are the people who worked with you once upon a time and you were their chief in the service where you worked in Zenica in 1993.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I met Amir [as interpreted] by chance on one occasion, but we did not talk about any details in connection with this. I only told him that I had been here and testified and that it was over, and that was all. I did not go into any details or enter into a discussion. I didn't feel it was necessary at all. I did not meet Mr. Adnan at all, and I never tried to do anything about this or in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Just an additional question about (redacted). Did he tell you whether he had made a statement to investigators of this Tribunal or didn't you talk about it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: He told me that he had also been contacted, but he didn't give me any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Could you just tell us when this was, approximately, this conversation of yours between the two testimonies?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it was perhaps two months after my testimony, but it's hard to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. So it may have been around April this year?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us try now to go back to the period of your service. Your service, as you said, lasted from January to March 1993, so I think you said it lasted for about three months.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, if you mean only that part of my task, so to speak. You are referring to the mission, what we are discussing right now. Yes. Yes. Well, then we can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please -- we shall come back to this event in greater detail later on, but can you just tell us in principle: The people whose task was to make the recordings of these conversations, did they make transcripts? The conversations that were recorded on tape, were they put down on paper? Was a transcript produced in written form?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Partly, so what was important was sent in the form of a report to the superior command. Not everything, of course; only what was most important, what was important in the then situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
