utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, I must remind you that this witness has already been cross-examined and it would not be fair to subject him to another cross-examination about all his evidence. The scope of this cross-examination has to be severely limited, and it is to do with the authenticity of the tape and the possibility that it's been tampered with by adding language to it or moving language on the tape about, that sort of suggestion and manipulation. Now, I'm not going to stop you asking some general questions, but that is the heart of it, and so we must restrict you to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. I fully accept what you say. I have to say, however, that in the meantime, we have received some statements from people who worked with Mr. Husic and who represented things slightly differently, and I felt it was my professional duty to ask him about it, if you will allow me. And one of those questions has to do with the transcripts because one of the persons whose statement we received said that the transcripts were made on several occasions. They put down transcripts in written form of the recordings, and the witness never said that. That's why I had to ask him. But I will not dwell on this long if you will only allow me to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One or two questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you have just said that reports were drawn up. We all know what the word "report" means. It's a kind of a cover note that you send with the tape. But I was referring to a transcript, that is, to taking down the speech, the language, and putting it down on paper. Were such transcripts ever made?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'll try to explain. General Hadzihasanovic, as my commander, was directly informed by me so he could hear the conversations that had been recorded. Of course not all of them, only the important ones. And later on he had the tape we are talking about. As for the transcripts that were part of the reports we submitted at that time to the General Staff, they were part of the reports that I sent to the superior command in Sarajevo. Transcripts that would be kept along with the recorded material was not made. What was made was only for the purposes of the report. That is my answer in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well, but we have to draw a distinction. One thing were the written notes that you received. I understand that. I am asking you about the records now because (redacted) said that, on several occasions, written transcripts were made which were delivered to you together with the tapes. So the conversation that was recorded was also put down on paper. That's my question: Where are these transcripts?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Of course, but, later, it was typed up in a file which was then transformed into a report and sent on to the superior command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So then, these transcripts should be somewhere? Where? In what department of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: At that time, the reports were sent directly to the intelligence administration of the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, where did the notes end up that were given to you by your people together with the tapes?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: We destroyed them. It was usually written on sheets of paper, and later on, as the service developed, part of this was probably preserved because then the logs started to be kept. But as far as I can remember, what they gave me on the sheets of paper and what was important for a transcript for the purposes of the report only, that paper was later destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell us, by the way, we agree that you do not know who is the author of this transcript that I have here. You can look at them. These are transcripts related to these tapes. You don't know who did that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that some service, perhaps translators here in The Hague, did it, because I, for instance, read those transcripts yesterday. And this is the material which I had an opportunity to see when I first testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. But I asked you where was this material sent, because we wrote to the federation army and, unfortunately, they did not supply us with the material that you mentioned and some other witnesses before you, but what can we do? And just one technical question more and then we shall move on to this specific issue. I don't think I shall have too many questions. The equipment that you had at your disposal at the time, which means in January, February 1993, it practically came down to a telephone and a simple answering machine or something like that. At least, that is what one of those men said.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was not a telephone. It was a device which could also be operated as an interphone. That is, in a way it was an answering machine which could receive the signal, and as an interphone, as a speaker phone, to transmit it; and from that device, then that signal could be sent on to some other telephone. Then we use it, use it only because of this interphone feature. It was very difficult, you know, to hear. That is, we had to hear. We did not have any sophisticated state-of-the-art equipment which would allow us to record directly. So, from the telephone line, from the telephone switch, we switched on this answering machine, and from that device, then it was -- the signal was sent on to a portable dictating machine or something like that, and that is how we recorded those conversations on a microtape. That is what I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Just one question more. This device or these devices, what source of energy did they use; normal electric energy?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it was 220, the voltage, so you had to use transformers, but of course, yes, they were electrical devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And that other device, tell us, the one that you used to copy this on other cassettes, did it also use the electrical energy as a source of energy?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: That was a small manual thing, and it used dry batteries. It was a very primitive way to do it, but there was no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. So let us, then, move on to the event we're particularly interested in, that alleged conversation on the 24th of January, 1993. We agree that one of your superiors gave you the cassette with the recorded conversation and an accompanying note; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, the cassette, yes. Was there an accompanying note? I'm not quite sure. Perhaps it was written subsequently, but there was the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I meant the subordinate, the transcript says wrongly, but somebody who worked for you, who did this for you, gave you this cassette?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And I didn't quite understand about the note. Did you get it immediately or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I cannot really say. I just don't remember whether the transcript was made straight away or not. I don't think so. If there was a transcript, then it must have been done subsequently. I believe I was given the first cassette only.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. But did you know if -- when that tape was made and who were the participants in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. I was made to understand that the conversation was very important, and that the conversation was -- that the participants were Kordic and Blaskic. And naturally, when I saw when it was about, I listened to it, and I notified my commander because, at that time, it was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you were explicitly told without any doubt whatsoever, without any room for doubt, that the conversation recorded was between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, I have to tell you, when you gave your first statement to the investigators on the 4th of December, 1999, that you said explicitly that one of your men handed the cassette over to you. That was passage 8 of your previous statement, and you said verbatim, "The information about the conversation recorded on a piece of paper included the date of the recording, which was the 24th of January, 1993, and it was said that the participants in the conversation were allegedly or reportedly Blaskic and Kordic." From what I've just read to you, it says that you said, and I can show it to you because that was your statement which I was given by the Prosecution, that the monitor who told you that as a matter of fact was not sure because the word "allegedly" or "reportedly" was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, you've been reading something at great length. In any event, this is nothing to do with the authenticity of the tape. This is part of the original cross-examination. Now, would you come to the authenticity of the tape. As I said, it's not fair on the witness to be subjected to a general cross-examination about his evidence. He's already been subjected to that. What you may ask and what you should ask is any question about the authenticity of the tape, that is, whether it's been manipulated or not. That is the whole issue, not a free-ranging, wide-ranging cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course, Your Honours, I understand what you are saying. But I think that these two things are inseparable because it begins with an alleged conversation and answer with a certain effect, hence my doubts and doubts of our Defence that part of that, of that conversation was fabricated, and I'm going to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you remember that conversation, Mr. Husic, that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you remember the tone? Was it serious, was it half jester, was it very serious? What was your impression about that? And yesterday you read the transcripts, you saw the vocabulary used.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I understand what you're asking me about, but was the tone and the conversation between two men that we are referring to, was it merry or not, I think that what was going on shows that it was very serious indeed. And all the other conversations, I suppose, confirm what was going on on the ground. Would you say that they said that it was "allegedly" then? Of course, it is very difficult to be sure, but were you in a situation to hear something that you've never heard before, you would have heard it. If you were in a situation and as it was at the time, you would realise who it was, what they were talking about, and what the intentions were behind it. So that conversation could sound as a joking conversation between the two of them, but I did not think so, not in the least. On the other hand, I was duty-bound to forward this information to my superior, to the commander, and give my -- voice my opinion that I do think that those were their intentions, and very serious ones. Of course, when you are in a situation to assess some facts, it is very difficult to be sure. One can hardly be ever sure about something 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Husic, you are a professional. You did that job. You had some experience; you did it professionally. Then at that time you were clear, as a professional, that it is only on the basis of the original recording that one can establish the authenticity of a conversation, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: But that is the original recording. Whether it was copied once or twice is irrelevant because it did not undergo any changes. Naturally, in assessing it, that is not the only thing that is considered as an element as it is all the available information that must be borne in mind. I cannot say that I'm an expert on that particular aspect, but I was an intelligence officer, I was trained for this, and that is what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Well, that is that part of your experience that I have in mind. You were asked by His Honour last time, 13.732, how is it that you kept this particular cassette which was a copy of the original microtape which contained the original recording. That is the reason for my additional question. It seemed to you that the substance of the conversation was so significant that you kept it as a souvenir and to train future personnel, yet not -- only the original can contain the authenticity, then how could you allow that the two -- how could you allow the destruction of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. microtape? You must have been aware that that was the original.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, we used microtapes only to record conversations. They were expendable stationery. We did not have enough of them, so we could not keep those conversations in their original form. And we did not even plan to keep all the conversations. This conversation was kept because it was very interesting and very important. Others were preserved and recorded on that particular tape because General Hadzihasanovic requested us to do that. That is when we made those two tapes. One of them is here. Now, the question, to my mind, is -- whether the original is on the microtape or this here is not a question because, for me, the material which is on this tape, the recorded conversation, is absolutely identical. The only question that may arise is the quality, because whenever one copies it, one loses some of the quality but not the substance of it. The fact that I kept only this conversation, and only this, is because it was something that was very interesting to me because that is something which is very -- which one very rarely has the opportunity to have. There are quite a number of other documents that can be kept, but I simply decided to keep this, for personal reasons only. And at that time, none of us could even guess or imagine. Perhaps we would have kept much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but I have to tell you what the Court expects of you, and I will tell you that we put it to you that there was never a conversation of precisely this content that is indicated in the transcript that you had the opportunity to read once again tomorrow [as interpreted], never in that form. So my question is: Can you, before this august court, confirm that this alleged conversation of 1993 is absolutely identical with what you read in the transcript yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: If that is what you're asking me, then I should hear the tape once again and read the transcript which you have before you. All I can do is confirm that that tape was never subjected to any tampering, any addition, any change, either by me or by anybody else. As long as I had it in my possession -- and we talked about this last time -- but I, of my own will, offered the second tape that I had also recorded on the eve of the day when I handed over that cassette to Mr. Mustafa Music, because I still wanted to keep it, and that is what I can confirm. You cannot ask me about every single word in that transcript. And the cassette, if you have to listen to it and read it, then I can say, "Yes, this is it," and "This is not it." But I am positive about what I'm saying, and that is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But we have to repeat it for the Court, so let us remind you. You answered my learned colleague's question, Bob Stein's, that you did not have the tape in your possession between the 4th of December, 1999 until a later date, that is, until about a week later, when you heard it again.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember. So bearing in mind what I read yesterday, between the 20th of November until the 4th of December, it was that period of time when I did not have the tape in my possession, the one that I turned over for the first time. The copy that I made on the 19th, that is, in the evening, copying that same tape, I did have it in my possession and I gave it the last time -- I handed it over the last time so that possibly you could see if any changes had been made on the tape that I had turned over on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Right. I don't really want to talk about this, because the expert witnesses talked about them and there were differences between those cassettes, but I don't really want to tire you with it anymore, and it will be the Court which will decide about this, because the Judges have heard the testimony. I'm asking you: As a professional, a professional who was trained for that particular job, will you agree with me that there are relatively easily accessible or relatively sophisticated computer programmes allowing to reproduce audio recordings, making all sorts of -- allowing all sorts of interventions, so on and so forth, and it is used in music, in making music recordings, so on and so forth; there can be no dispute about this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, but then I could sing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And me too. Right. I will not ask some of the questions, in compliance with your instruction, but I shall merely like to show Z2801.3. I have some copies for the witness on the ELMO and I should like to show this exhibit to the witness, Z2801.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you have before you this. Do you remember it? It was on the cover, or what shall I call it? Well, you know, that bit of paper which comes with tapes where you can write down whatever facts. Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A while ago, we said what is alleged and what is not alleged. You understand it is difficult to be absolutely sure. But there is not a single question mark, except on page B -- on side B, under 2. There we have a question mark. All the rest are simply statements of conversations. So that caution that "alleged." This is something that we don't see from here, because there are no question marks anywhere, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: When I did this, of course, I listened to the recording and I noted down the conversations and what was there. This here, where there is a question mark, I could not establish who the participants were. So this is my handwriting, this is what I did at the time, and I was positive about what I was doing, because I couldn't really give my commander a tape just like that, a tape without any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But under B3, if I understand it properly, this is Nakic and T. Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And in the transcript, we can see that it is a certain Franjo. That is what you decided, I suppose, with Colonel Blaskic; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: However, what stuck in my memory is that this index is not all that precise. It does not quite tally with what is on the tapes. It's not that we have 11 recordings on the A side and the rest on the B side, if I remember well. Is this only a list of conversations, regardless of the side, or did you try to be accurate, marking precisely which is which?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I noted down those conversations as they followed one another, that sequence. If you're asking me, I was listening to them and I was writing down what I heard. Whether somebody else listened to that and acquired a different impression, I can't say. But what you see here is what I wrote and it dates back to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. But let us go back to this. I think in the transcript my colleague draws my attention. We said that under B3 you said it was Franjo Nakic and Tihomir Blaskic's conversation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Because the transcript wasn't clear. That is why I wanted to ask about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have said, I would have some more questions, but in view of the limited range of the cross-examination, I put my views to the witness and he responded, and I do not wish to keep either the Court or the witness at it any longer, and therefore I conclude with this. Thank you very much. Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tape recordings that you made on the ordinary-size tape were made with your battery-operated machine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you mean this tape, this device was an electrically-fed device. It was the conventional type. But the reproduction was from a battery-operated device, dictating machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So to make sure I've got this, the microcassettes were produced on a battery-operated machine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. This device, which is a portable device, that was -- that used electricity. But when I listen to the cassettes, I cannot listen to them using that device, because it is being used; it is working. So I had to use another one. So I reproduced it to a dictating machine, from which I could copy then -- copied then on a big tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so the intermediate machine was battery driven, was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second thing is, just to cover a matter of detail: The tape that you first produced via the officials in your department to Mr. Lopez-Terres, which is the one for which -- this is the JPS jacket -- had that been in your possession throughout from the time when you first recorded it until the time when you handed it to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the second tape that you produced at Court from your briefcase or somewhere, the one you kept for yourself, had that been in your possession from the moment when you first recorded it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you, incidentally, now remember the make of that tape that you produced at Court on the last occasion? If you can, tell us; if you can't, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think it was Maxell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You first heard the conversations when you heard them on microcassettes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now know you were personally responsible for the taping thereafter, up and until the final production of these two tapes. What's being raised with you, so that you can be quite clear about the suggestion, is that you, alone or with others, in some way have corrupted those tapes to make them say things that the speakers never said. Is there any truth in that suggestion which, however decorously, is nevertheless being raised?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. All this is genuine, as it was recorded. The material which I got and which I prepared, I never made any changes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, are you still in the services yourself?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the present rank of?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you're able to tell us, your present posting is where? If you don't want to tell us, it doesn't matter, but if you can just tell us what your current posting is.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm with the defence naval attache of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the United States of America; military naval attache at the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need ask of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, thank you for coming back to answer those questions. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It being 4.00, the Court is not minded to sit much later. There are two matters, though, I want to deal with in closed session. Before we do, we ought to have in mind what we're going to deal with tomorrow. First of all, perhaps Witness AO, what is the position about him? He's not -- he failed to catch the plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He hasn't responded. The position is he hasn't responded or has declined to come. It may be further efforts will be made and those executing the process will be able to inform me. I can simply keep you informed and, in due course, if he simply doesn't turn up, I shall be inviting the Court to consider taking action in respect of him, but for the time being, the position is as I've stated it. It's always rather difficult to get comprehensive accounts from this distance of what happens on the ground, but as I understand it, opportunities were available and weren't taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to -- yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would not like to be impolite, but your decision was made long ago, and we have a schedule day by day. And if the witness has not appeared so far, I don't see when the witness can possibly come, because every week we have a full schedule; every day has been planned ahead. And I would not like to have to deal with this on the last day of our case. I think enough has been done to make the witness come. He came here the first time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The trial Chamber is concerned, as Mr. Naumovski says, about the timetable and the effects of witnesses not appearing upon it. You'll give us a report tomorrow, Mr. Nice, and then we'll have to consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow we will consider the position with regard to some of the applications which have been made as far as we can, certainly about witnesses, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one particular -- in fact, if it's not impertinent -- there's one particular witness who it seems conveniently falls to be dealt with in argument tomorrow. His travel arrangements are, I believe, currently Tuesday for Wednesday, so it would obviously be helpful to know in advance what the position is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You were going to tell us the names of the witnesses on whom you were going to rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can tell you the ones I know about -- I've got knowledge about at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be better if we can do that in closed session because I'm not sure whether either of the last two names are going to require any form of protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into closed session.
